text: In the 1970s Poland was ruled by one party and was under the power of the Soviet Union.
Armies led by the Soviet Union had crushed the Hungarian Uprising and the Prague Spring.
src: In the 1970s Poland was a satellite state of the Soviet Union, ruled in practice by one party
Soviet-led invasions had crushed the Hungarian Uprising of 1956 and the Prague Spring of 1968

text: In August 1980, workers at the shipyard in Gdańsk went on strike after Anna Walentynowicz lost her job.
The government agreed to let them form Solidarity, a free trade union, a group that speaks up for workers.
src: Born of the August 1980 strike at the Gdańsk Shipyard / The dismissal of Anna Walentynowicz sets off a strike at the Gdańsk Shipyard
the government signs the agreement allowing Solidarity to exist / the right to exist as an independent, self-governing trade union

text: Lech Wałęsa led the union, and by 1981 it had 10 million members.
In December 1981 the government brought in martial law, strict rule by force, and jailed the union’s leaders.
src: Lech Wałęsa led the movement from its birth / Membership peaked at 10 million in September 1981
On 13 December 1981 the government of General Wojciech Jaruzelski imposed martial law / in December martial law is imposed and the union’s leaders are jailed

text: Solidarity carried on in secret, and in 1983 Wałęsa won the Nobel Peace Prize.
Solidarity always tried to reach its aims without violence.
src: Operating underground, Solidarity survived / In 1983 he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize
Solidarity advocated non-violence / it always pursued its aims with a high degree of nonviolent discipline

text: In 1989 Solidarity won almost every seat it could stand for, and this helped set off the Revolutions of 1989.
Today Solidarity is a trade union again; in 2010 it had more than 400,000 members.
src: The Round Table Talks of 1989 led to semi-free elections that Solidarity swept / Solidarity won 99 of the 100 Senate seats and all 161 contestable seats in the Sejm / helped set off the Revolutions of 1989
After 1989 Solidarity became a more traditional trade union / In 2010 the union had more than 400,000 members
